summary: Hexagonal reinforced-concrete light first lit September 30, 1912 on Vancouver Island's Juan de Fuca coast. Unstaffed since 1989; owned and run by a society since 2015.

lens.where: Sooke Region Museum; a panel can be viewed by appointment (LighthouseFriends)

structures.type: hexagonal reinforced concrete with six buttresses
structures.note: Heights differ between sources: Society 12.5 m; LighthouseFriends about 20 m.
Keeper's dwelling intentionally burned January 9, 1986 (LighthouseFriends). A modern bungalow built 1964 was burned in the mid-1990s.
Flat-roofed concrete block building that replaced the 1925 building.

access.note: Site open to the public every day. Walking trail from the parking lot at the end of Sheringham Point Road (about 200 m, then a steeper 300 m to the tower). Tower interior and engine room closed for safety. The Society says this trail is the only legal access.

visit.note: Visitor centre staffed by volunteers on a limited basis (Society). Current hours given as 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. (Society; seasonal changes).

facts.agency: Canadian Coast Guard (aid to navigation); site owned, operated and cared for by the Sheringham Point Lighthouse Preservation Society since 2015

events.note: Hexagonal reinforced-concrete tower built under contract; design of William P. Anderson
Eustace Arden moved in as first keeper in 1912
Lit for the first time on September 30, 1912 by Eustace Arden
Third-order Fresnel lens, floated on mercury, clockwork-driven
Bark Anna Barnard struck rocks a few miles from Sheringham Point on February 26, 1862 (LighthouseFriends)
Valencia wreck (January 22, 1906; 137 lost) at Pachena Point prompted new aids along the coast, including Sheringham Point
Two-tone diaphone foghorn, diesel-powered, added with its fog-alarm building
Site enlarged by 1.7 acres; surveillance building for armed forces watching for enemy incursions
Fog-alarm building replaced with flat-roofed concrete-block structure
Fresnel lens replaced by an electric rotating lens (Crouse-Hinds DCB36); original lens to Sooke Region Museum
Original keeper's dwelling intentionally burned January 9, 1986, after the assistant keeper's post was abolished
De-staffed in August 1989 (LighthouseFriends); the Society says automated during the 1980s and de-staffed in 1989
Government declares the site excess to its program requirements (January 2003); Preservation Society formed
Government of Canada declares the lighthouse and most others surplus
Designated a National Heritage Lighthouse in June 2015 (Society); LighthouseFriends says 2015
Legal title to the lighthouse and surrounding land transferred to the Society in October 2015

keepers.name: Eustace Travanion Arden
keepers.note: First keeper; lit the light September 30, 1912. Spelled 'Travonian' by the Society and 'Travanion' by LighthouseFriends. Retired February 18, 1946 (LighthouseFriends). Listed against Sheringham Point in the Department's 1916 keeper table.

keepers.name: Thomas Charles Cross
keepers.note: Temporary keeper for about four months while a replacement for Arden was found (Society).

keepers.name: Alfred Dickenson
keepers.note: Full name Alfred Stamp Dickenson (Society). Retired 1948.

keepers.name: Thomas Westhead
keepers.note: Retired 1959 (Society). One Society caption spells the name Westead.

keepers.name: Frederick Arthur Mountain
keepers.note: Known as Fred Mountain. The Society gives his death at the station in 1967; LighthouseFriends and the Sooke historian say Bruton arrived in 1968 after Mountain died there.

keepers.name: James D. Bruton
keepers.note: Known as Jim Bruton. The Society gives 1967; LighthouseFriends and the Sooke historian give 1968. Lens replaced in 1976 during his tenure (Society).

keepers.name: Kurt Cehak
keepers.note: Took charge after Bruton retired until de-staffing (LighthouseFriends).

keepers.name: Erika Cehak
keepers.note: Officially listed as the last head lightkeeper for the last six months of the Cehaks' tenure, because labour rules stopped Kurt Cehak's rehire (Society). The Society calls her the only woman to hold that post at Sheringham.

wrecks.outcome: Struck rocks a few miles from Sheringham Point at night in fog. Captain swam ashore; the cook and a seaman drowned; five men climbed the mast and waded ashore at low tide. Survivors, helped by First Nation people, were taken to Victoria (LighthouseFriends).

corrections.why: The Society says the site is open to the public every day; only the tower interior and engine room are closed. The record's 'closed' comes from the Lighthouse Directory, which the Society's current page supersedes.
Grounds open daily (Society). Tower interior closed.

corrections.proposed: non-profit society (Sheringham Point Lighthouse Preservation Society), title transferred October 2015
corrections.why: Society home page and history: owned, operated and cared for by the Society; legal title transferred October 2015. The light remains on the Coast Guard's list of lights.
De-staffed in August 1989 (LighthouseFriends; Society). The 1986 date is when the assistant keeper's post was abolished and the dwelling burned.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Record gives automation in 1986 (Wikidata). LighthouseFriends says the assistant's post and dwelling ended in 1986 and the station was de-staffed in August 1989. The Society says automated in the 1980s and de-staffed in 1989. The story gives 1989 for de-staffing and notes the 1986 change.
Society: designated June 2015. LighthouseFriends: 2015. Wikipedia gives 16 April 2015 (not cited; lead only). The story says 2015 with the Society's month.

The Society says a two-tone diaphone foghorn was added in 1925 and powered by a diesel engine. LighthouseFriends says the original steam fog horn was replaced around 1925 by a diaphone powered by compressed air from oil engines. The story gives both.

The Society's visit page gives current hours of 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. with seasonal changes; a site-hours box on the Society's keepers page reads 9:00 am to 6:00 pm. The story gives both and does not choose.

notes_for_editor: (1) Tower height disagrees: record 19.5 m (Wikipedia-derived); Society 12.5 m; LighthouseFriends about 20 m. The story gives both and does not choose. (2) Bruton's start: Society 1967, LighthouseFriends and the Sooke historian 1968; Mountain's end: Society 1967 (death), LighthouseFriends 1968 implied. Both shown. (3) The 1916 keeper table is OCR text with the column split. The story now dates it to the fiscal year 1914-15 (the Forty-Eighth Annual Report, Sessional Paper No. 21, printed 1916; the cover of the OCR says so). E. T. Arden is matched by position: the OCR shows 26 station names and 26 keeper names in the same order, so Arden is 16th, as 'Sheringham point' is 16th. The Society's record (Arden at the station 1912-1946) agrees. The page image was not viewed in this pass (the archive.org image endpoint returned only the cover). The appointment-date column is split by the OCR and is not used. (4) LighthouseFriends' cost figures ($8,745; $7,609.50; $4,898.49) are quoted from the Department report; the two cents amounts appear in the OCR of the 1914 volume, but the row was not matched by position, so the figures are attributed to LighthouseFriends. (5) The contractor's city differs: LighthouseFriends says Victoria; the OCR of the 1913 works table reads 'Vancouver' in the column. The story gives only the name. (6) Anna Barnard (1862) rests on LighthouseFriends alone; no contemporary newspaper was found. The Society and LighthouseFriends are both copyrighted sites; quotes are kept to short phrases. (7) The keeper list is not from a roster: Arden, Cross, Dickenson, Westhead, Mountain, Bruton and the Cehaks are named by the Society and LighthouseFriends, and Arden also in the 1916 table; spellings vary (Travonian/Travanion; Westhead/Westead; Fred/Frederick Mountain). (8) People who may be alive: Kurt Cehak is alive per the Society; only role and years are used for post-1960 keepers, and the Society's personal anecdotes are left out. (9) Visibility: the Society's 'almost 25 km' and the Coast Guard's 9 nautical mile nominal range are different measures; both are given. (10) Wikipedia's keeper list and automation dates (1988; Bruton 1968; Westhead to 1959 vs open) were not cited; they are leads only. (11) The record's 'access: closed' and 'ownership: federal' are corrected above from the Society's current pages. (12) The Society calls Anderson 'chief lighthouse designer' for the Department of Fisheries and Oceans; Parks Canada and the 1915 report give Chief Engineer of the Department of Marine. The story uses the latter. (13) The 1925 foghorn: the Society says it was added and diesel-powered; LighthouseFriends says it replaced the steam horn and used oil engines. Both are given in the story. (14) Site hours: the visit page says 9 a.m. to 7 p.m.; a box on the keepers page says 9:00 am to 6:00 pm. Both are given.
